# Prepare Talking Points for Your Next Performance Review with Grok

> **In short:** Grok can help you turn a messy brain-dump of this quarter's work into clear, confident talking points for your performance review. You list what you did in plain language, then Grok groups it into themes, picks out wins, and rewrites it the way you'd actually say it.

Performance reviews are one of those things most people dread — not because the work was bad, but because we forget half of what we did. Three months is a long time. By the time the meeting arrives, the small wins, the tricky problems, the saved-the-day moments are all blurred. A short session with Grok before the meeting changes that. You give it the raw material in your own words, and it hands you back a clean set of talking points you can actually use.

## Before you start
- A free or paid **Grok account** (available through the X platform and the Grok website — both work for this task).
- A rough **brain-dump list** of things you remember doing this quarter: projects, problems solved, meetings, compliments you got. Even a messy list is fine.
- About **20–30 minutes**. Five minutes to dump your thoughts into a note, and another 15 to work through the steps below.
- Optional: a **target role or goal** you want the review to set you up for (a raise, a promotion, a new responsibility). It helps Grok steer the talking points.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh Grok conversation
Open Grok in a browser or in the X app, then start a **new chat** — don't keep adding to an old conversation, because Grok only pays attention to the messages in the current thread. A new chat gives you a clean slate so all of Grok's energy goes toward your review prep.
💬 Example: type **"Help me prep talking points for my upcoming performance review."** as the very first message.
You'll know it worked when Grok responds with a short, friendly acknowledgement and asks a clarifying question or two — that's exactly what you want.

## Step 2 — Dump your quarter into the chat
In the same chat, paste (or type) a **brain-dump of everything you did** this quarter. Don't try to make it pretty — bullet points, fragments, half-sentences, dates, all welcome. Think of it like telling a friend over coffee what kept you busy. The richer the dump, the better Grok's output. If you don't remember something, skip it; you can add more later.
💬 Example: *"Q3 stuff I remember: shipped the onboarding redesign in July, fixed the broken import flow that was bugging sales for months, mentored two new hires (Priya and Tom), ran the customer interviews for the new dashboard, wrote the Q3 retro doc, picked up the Friday newsletter for a month when Sara was out, got a thank-you from the Head of Support about the import fix."*
You'll know it worked when Grok confirms it has your list and either asks a follow-up or starts reorganizing it.

## Step 3 — Ask Grok to group it into themes
Now ask Grok to **sort your brain-dump into 3–5 themes** like "shipped work", "people and mentorship", "cross-team help". Grouping helps you see the shape of your quarter at a glance, and it makes the talking points easier to remember in the meeting. If Grok's categories feel off, tell it to regroup using different labels — for example, by project name, by skill, or by impact.
💬 Example: *"Group these into 3–5 themes that show the shape of my quarter. Use plain labels a manager would understand."*
You'll know it worked when you see a clean list of themes with your items underneath each one, and you can quickly tell whether anything important is missing.

## Step 4 — Pull out your top 5 wins
Ask Grok to **pick your strongest 5 wins** from the dump and write each one as a short, confident sentence — the way you'd actually say it out loud, not the way you'd write it in a report. This is the heart of the prep: when the manager says "so what did you do?", these five sentences are what you want ready.
💬 Example: *"Pick my top 5 wins from this list and write each as one sentence I can say in the meeting. Start each sentence with 'I', and add a result or number when one is in my list."*
You'll know it worked when you read the five sentences back to yourself and think, "yes, that's me."

## Step 5 — Prep for the harder questions
Ask Grok to **play your manager** for two minutes. Give it your role and one or two weaknesses or gaps you actually had this quarter, and have it ask you the tough questions a real reviewer might ask ("what would you do differently?", "where did you fall short?"). Then practice answering out loud. This is the step most people skip — and it's the one that makes you walk in calm instead of caught off-guard.
💬 Example: *"Act like my manager. I'm a senior product designer. One thing I struggled with this quarter was giving critical feedback to a peer. Ask me 3 tough questions about that, one at a time, and wait for my answers."*
You'll know it worked when you can answer the questions without freezing, and you have a one-sentence version of each answer ready.

## Step 6 — Save the output somewhere you'll actually open it
Copy the final talking points into a **note on your phone**, a doc, or a calendar event for the day of the review. Don't leave them buried in the chat — on the morning of the meeting, you'll want to skim them in 60 seconds. If your company uses a review form, paste the wins into the form fields now while they're fresh.
💬 Example: create a note titled **"Review — talking points"** with your five wins at the top, the themes below, and the tough-question answers at the bottom.
You'll know it worked when you can open your phone on the way into the meeting and have everything you need in under a minute.

## Common mistakes
- **Writing the brain-dump too cleanly.** If you spend 20 minutes polishing it before pasting, you've used up the energy Grok should be spending. Messy in, tidy out — that's the point.
- **Asking Grok to lie or exaggerate.** If something wasn't a win, don't dress it up. Managers notice, and AI-assisted exaggeration reads fast. Feed in what actually happened; Grok will frame it well without inventing impact.
- **Skipping Step 5.** The five wins feel like enough — until your manager asks the one question you didn't prepare for. Two minutes of practice in the chat saves you ten minutes of sweating in the room.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same brain-dump trick works for a parent-teacher meeting, a doctor's appointment recap, or a "what did I do all year" journal entry — any time you need to remember a lot of small things at once.
- **For your business or work:** beyond reviews, this is a quarterly ritual you can run every three months in 20 minutes, so you never again walk into a review scrambling to remember July. Pair it with a Friday-afternoon "monthly brag list" and you'll never start from zero.
- **If you're just getting started:** open Grok right now and dump everything you did this week into it. You'll be surprised how much comes back when an AI hands it to you in tidy sentences.

## Try it now
Open Grok and paste in just **three things you did this week**, however rough. Ask it to rewrite them as three "I" statements. That's it — under two minutes, and you'll feel the difference between "uh, I worked on stuff" and "I shipped X, I fixed Y, I led Z."
